newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-10 Russian firms in hunt for Iraq oil deals.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-10 Russian firms in hunt for Iraq oil deals.

text.p: Russia looks set to boost the amount of Iraqi oil it lifts under the second phase of the U.N. "oil-for-food" scheme, with 10 companies looking for a slice of exports compared with eight in the first phase.

With just two days to go before Iraqi oil is due to return to world markets under the U.N. programme, eight Russian firms are already in Baghdad for talks. Two deals have been signed, and several more are expected by the end of the week.

Warm political ties between Moscow and Baghdad promise to secure a smooth passage for Russian negotiators, in contrast to British and Japanese firms apparently excluded from the second phase, for what Mitsubishi called "political reasons."
Yuri Agababov, deputy general director of Russian oil trader Zarubezhneft, which is coordinating Russian purchases of Iraqi crude, said two deals had been signed between Iraq and Russia.
"Two deals were signed in Baghdad on Saturday," Agababov told Reuters. "Zarubezhneft signed a deal to lift 5.55 million barrels, and Alfa-Eko another for 2.65 million barrels."
Under the first 180-day programme Zarubezhneft had a contract for 3.65 million barrels. Alfa-Eko was the biggest Russian lifter of Iraqi oil with contracts for 6.89 million barrels.

Russian oil traders said it was too early to compare individual companies' allocations, because each company could sign more than one deal and some Russian firms lifted Iraqi oil on the spot market as well as through contracts.
But the general opinion among participating Russian firms was that overall volumes would increase this time round.
"I think Russia will be looking to increase its share of Iraqi oil under the new deal," said a trader at one of the firms involved in the first phase of the programme.

"There may be a change in allocations for each company -- some may get more, others less. We are generally looking to get around the same quantity, but certainly the same kind of crude and to the same destination," he added.
Zarubezhneft's Agababov said the list of Russian companies taking part in the second stage of the deal was set to grow to at least 10 from eight in the first stage.

"All eight companies that took part in the first phase want to continue to lift Iraqi oil," he said. "And the next stage is that two more companies -- ONAKO and SIDANKO -- are likely to buy Iraqi oil, taking the total to 10."
Iraq created room for higher liftings for political allies after it blocked participation by British and Japanese firms.
Anglo-Dutch Royal Dutch/Shell, British Petroleum Co Plc and Japan's Mitsubishi Corp confirmed Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organisation would not renew contracts.
The three firms had deals to lift 10.8 million barrels under the first phase of the plan.
The oil-for-food programme allows Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months. It went into effect last December and was renewed for another six months on June 8.
But the second phase is behind schedule after a two-month delay to allow modifications to aid distribution plans.
Russia was the single biggest lifter in the first phase, taking 28.54 million barrels, or 23 percent of total Iraqi exports under the deal.
Politics as much as economics are expected to play their part in the second phase, analysts said.
"I wouldn't be surprised if Russia gets more oil this time," said a Western banking analyst specialising in Russian oil.
"(Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny) Primakov has excellent connections with top authorities in Iraq and among Russian firms positioned to handle the lifting deals," she added.
Primakov, a Middle East specialist, has called Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz his "old comrade". Russian firms are also looking to develop Iraqi oil production.

Russia's biggest oil company, LUKoil, has a 52.5 percent stake in a $4 billion, 23-year output-sharing agreement in Western Qurnah. Output from the field could reach one million barrels per day in four to six years after work begins.
